items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 3.7 Flash, an improved AI model for coding and agents with better accuracy and lower cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing Gemini 3.7 Flash
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 3.7 Flash, an enhanced AI model designed to improve coding, knowledge work, and web development workflows. This update follows the Gemini 3.6 Flash release by three weeks and offers better debugging, higher code accuracy, and improved performance in generating production-ready code, all at half the previous cost per million tokens.

Gemini 3.7 Flash also advances capabilities in web development by producing more functional layouts and feature-complete applications with fewer prompts, and it shows stronger reasoning and accuracy in complex fields like finance, law, and biosciences. The model is integrated into Gemini Spark, Google's personal AI agent, enhancing its efficiency in knowledge work and tool use across Google Workspace apps.

The release includes updated safety safeguards against misuse in chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cyber domains. Gemini 3.7 Flash is available to developers, enterprises, and individuals through various Google platforms, aiming to provide cost-effective, production-ready AI agents with improved precision and developer experience.

items.title: Cerebras and OpenAI launch Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol, delivering up to 750 tokens per second with no quality loss, initially for select customers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast
items.summary:
Cerebras and OpenAI have introduced Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol, a new service tier in the OpenAI API that accelerates output speeds up to 750 tokens per second without compromising quality. This mode is initially available to select customers and aims to support time-sensitive, mission-critical applications by providing significantly faster AI inference.

Benchmark tests show GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast completing complex tasks like Humanity's Last Exam in just over 11 hours, compared to over 78 hours for comparable models, achieving nearly seven times faster performance with similar accuracy. The technology leverages Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine architecture to overcome data movement bottlenecks common in GPU-based inference, enabling rapid processing for high-stakes use cases such as legal, financial, and engineering workflows.

Ultrafast mode is expected to enhance productivity by enabling real-time AI insights and faster response times in critical scenarios like cybersecurity and service outage management. OpenAI and Cerebras highlight that this advancement allows users to focus on complex problems while maintaining parallel processing for routine tasks, potentially transforming how AI agents are integrated into workflows requiring immediate, high-quality intelligence.

items.title: Netlify tests identical prompts across 11 AI models, revealing significant differences in output and credit usage for web app generation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Choosing an AI model: one prompt, 11 models, different results
items.summary:
Netlify has partnered with OpenRouter to offer access to a wide range of AI models through its AI Gateway and Agent Runners, enabling developers to build or iterate on projects using various coding models. They conducted tests using the same prompts across 11 different models to evaluate differences in functionality, design, and credit consumption for generating web applications.

The tests focused on three use cases: a static site for a coffee shop, a multi-user to-do list app with database integration, and a recipe suggestion app using AI. Netlify used its AXIS tool to automatically evaluate model performance based on correct functionality rather than design aesthetics. The results highlighted how different models handle tasks and resource usage, providing insights for developers to choose models that balance cost and capability according to their needs.

items.title: Analysis: Text AI watermarks face inherent challenges and are likely to remain easy to remove despite EU AI Act requirements [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Text AI watermarks will always be trivial to remove
items.summary:
The European Union AI Act, enforceable from August 2026, mandates that all AI-generated text outputs must be detectable via watermarks. However, watermarking text is a complex problem because text is a compressed medium where subtle changes can degrade quality or be easily altered, making robust watermarking difficult to achieve. Google’s SynthID is one known approach that embeds detectable patterns in token selection probabilities, but such methods can be fragile and computationally expensive to verify.

The article explains that unlike images, text watermarking cannot rely on imperceptible noise, and attempts to embed watermarks risk compromising output quality or being removed by minor edits. It also discusses alternative detection methods, such as model-based verification, which are impractical at scale. The challenges suggest that while watermarking AI-generated text is a regulatory requirement, effective and tamper-proof solutions remain elusive, raising questions about enforcement and compliance in the AI industry.

items.summary: AI text watermarking embeds subtle, statistically detectable patterns within AI-generated text by influencing word choice probabilities during generation, allowing identification without visible changes. This technique, used by models like Google's Gemini and Claude since 2024 and 2026 respectively, relies on a secret key to bias word selection and later detect the watermark by analyzing word distributions. The watermark survives copying and pasting but can be disrupted by editing, which breaks the runs of original wording needed for detection.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic Models Can Be Cheaper to Use Than Chinese Ones, Study Finds
items.summary:
A recent analysis is challenging the idea that Chinese-made AI is cheaper than offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic. 

AlphaSense, a software firm that sells AI-powered search and market-research tools, released a study that found proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic are actually cheaper for performing some tasks, compared to open-weight models from leading Chinese developers. (AlphaSense used the models through cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft as well as Cerebras.)

Testing a range of models to search through and analyze its trove of financial data, AlphaSense found that GPT-5.6 Sol, the most advanced OpenAI model, and Opus 4.8, one of Anthropic’s most advanced models, generated better answers at a lower cost than models from two of China’s top AI labs: Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.2.

Comparing the cost effectiveness of different models can be tricky. Looking just at the price of the tokens—the units of text or images that AI ingests and generates—can give the misleading impression that open-source or open-weight models are always cheaper. Moonshot charges $15 per 1 million tokens of output from Kimi K3, while the comparable charge is $25 for Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 and $30 for OpenAI’s Sol. Some research indicates that can lead to real savings: AI benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis ranks Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 as significantly cheaper than the two U.S. models for accomplishing the same set of tasks, for example.

But the AlphaSense study, released earlier this month, echoes contentions from some American AI executives, who argue that greater intelligence can make the U.S. models more cost-effective despite their higher prices per token.

Bret Taylor, chairman of OpenAI’s board and co-founder of AI customer-service startup Sierra, said in a CNBC interview late last month that frontier models are cheaper and more efficient than open source ones because they use fewer tokens to answer a question or accomplish a task. 

The comment came after the release of Kimi K3, which performed comparably to leading U.S. models on some benchmarks, spurred worries that open models could erode the competitive positions of OpenAI and Anthropic, whose pricey models and coding tools have been pushing up enterprises’ AI bills. (Already, I’ve reported, companies are beginning to turn to open models for coding to bring down their AI costs).

AlphaSense asked each model 246 financial analysis questions that involved reviewing its mass of data, including earnings reports, investor call transcripts, SEC filings, news articles and more. The test questions included asking models to analyze commentary from pharmaceutical companies, to generate rundowns of major acquisitions by waste management giant Clean Harbors, and to analyze sales growth estimates by Wall Street analysts for luxury retailer Burberry. AlphaSense’s team scored the models based on the quality of their answers, such as whether any numbers used were from the correct time frame and whether they referenced multiple analysts’ perspectives.

AlphaSense found that the median cost of using GPT 5.6 Sol was about 13% lower than Kimi K3, while its quality score was around 20% higher. Similarly, Opus 4.8 was about half the cost of Kimi K3 but notched a quality score that was 13% higher. The difference was even starker with GLM 5.2, which was about twice the cost of Kimi K3 but ranked worse in terms of quality.

“Some of the more expensive models, the ones that look more expensive based on just their price per token, actually ended up being less costly because they were more efficient in using tokens,” AlphaSense CEO Jack Kokko told me.

Still, Kokko said, the ideal approach could involve a mixture of models. AlphaSense gets the best performance overall with its generative AI search tool by using its own “harness” software, which includes a router that can pick the best AI model for different parts of queries. For example, the router might select a smarter, more expensive model to plan how a question should be answered, and a smaller, cheaper model to carry out that plan. That lowers the cost per question significantly, he said.

To be sure, open models still have advantages. Because anyone can download them, a company can theoretically run them on its own server chips—if the company has enough of them—freeing it from paying per-token prices to other companies altogether. And while financial analysis is a domain that benefits from more intelligent models, weaker open models could be sufficient for handling simple tasks, such as summarizing emails.

That's precisely why model routing firms such as OpenRouter are having their day in the sun.

Rocket Drew contributed reporting.

items.originalTitle: Why The AI Compute Crunch Is Hitting Neolabs Especially Hard
items.summary:
The AI chip shortage is causing headaches for tech giants such as OpenAI. Among those hardest hit, though, are the startups trying to build their own AI models—so-called neolabs that need to use their limited funding to secure access to enormous clusters of graphics processing units for the compute-intensive task of model training.

“It’s like VC currency right now to know the current price of GPUs,” said Evan Morikawa, who recently finished talking with about 17 different AI cloud providers in search of compute for his startup Generalist, which trains AI models for robotics.

Morikawa compared searching for AI chips to exploring distant lands: “At a San Francisco dinner party, this is the equivalent of returning from the Far East,” he joked.

Startups training their own models require hundreds or thousands of GPUs or similar AI chips. When Morikawa was in the market for hundreds of chips last winter, he said cloud computing providers were offering contracts at reasonable prices with durations as short as 1 year. Six months into a 1-year contract, Generalist needed more compute, so Morikawa set out again to hunt for around a thousand chips.

items.summary:
Anthropic's Fable 5 is considered the most powerful AI model on the market, but U.S. companies are barely buying it. According to Ramp data, Fable 5 accounts for only six percent of Anthropic tokens sold. The model's steep price tag suggests corporate AI spending may have hit a ceiling, at least as long as performance gains don't translate into measurable everyday value.
